analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal firearms owner license, universal background checks, an assault weapons ban, and gun violence prevention funding.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees on December 5, 2023, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a federal license to own a gun or ammunition, requiring applicants to be 21, pass a background check, complete safety training, and submit a photograph. It would require background checks on nearly all gun sales with a 7-business-day waiting period, ban assault weapons and silencers with buy-back funding, expand domestic violence protections, raise excise taxes on firearms, and make gun trace data usable in lawsuits. It would also fund community violence intervention programs and gun violence research.
analysis.who_benefits: People at risk of gun violence, including victims of domestic abuse, school communities, and residents of high-violence neighborhoods. Lawful buyers who would benefit from consistent training and safety standards, and local organizations that would receive violence intervention grants.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People at risk of gun violence

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal firearm owner's license: applicants must be 21, pass a background check, complete written and hands-on safety training, and submit a photograph; licenses last 10 years and can be denied by a court if the applicant poses a risk to public safety

Requires background checks for nearly all firearm transfers, including private sales, with limited exceptions for immediate family gifts and temporary range use, and imposes a 7-business-day waiting period on purchases
Expands federal protections for domestic violence victims by extending firearm prohibitions to dating partners and people convicted of misdemeanor stalking
Bans new sales of assault weapons and large-capacity magazines and of firearm silencers, and directs Byrne grant funds toward buy-back programs for grandfathered weapons and accessories

Reforms gun dealers with security, inspection, employee background check, and lost-and-stolen reporting requirements, requires secure gun storage, and directs the Consumer Product Safety Commission to set standards for gun locks and safes
Creates a community violence intervention grant program and dedicated funding for research on gun violence prevention

analysis.who_pays: Lawful gun owners, who would face licensing, training, and storage requirements backed by civil penalties and criminal exposure; the firearms industry, which would face new bans, taxes, and legal exposure; and taxpayers, who would fund the grant programs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun owners and the firearms industry

drawbacks.text: Unlicensed possession of a firearm or ammunition would become a federal offense punishable by up to 2 years in prison, and the license requirement would take effect 2 years after enactment, meaning currently lawful owners would face a new federal crime if they did not comply

The ATF could ask a federal court to deny or revoke a license based on a 'preponderance of the evidence' showing the applicant could potentially create a public safety risk, a standard critics would call too loose for taking away a constitutional right

The 7-business-day waiting period applies to all sales, delaying purchases even when an instant background check clears immediately, and secure storage violations carry a $500 civil penalty per violation and up to 5 years in prison if a minor or prohibited person obtains the gun

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pursues gun violence prevention on nearly every available lever at once: licensing, background checks, waiting periods, bans, taxes, dealer regulation, and prevention grants. Supporters would point to the domestic violence, storage, and community intervention provisions as broadly beneficial; opponents' strongest fair objection is the sweep itself — a federal license to own any gun or ammunition, backed by criminal penalties, a relatively loose 'unsuitability' standard for denial, and a ban on a popular class of firearms — which is why it drew no Republican support. The bill never advanced far enough for the tradeoffs to be tested in committee or on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced, none of them ever voted on it, and it died when the Congress ended two years later.

narrative.text: Rep. Hank Johnson (D-GA) introduced the Gun Violence Prevention and Community Safety Act of 2023 in the House on December 5, 2023
The bill was referred the same day to the Judiciary, Ways and Means, and Energy and Commerce committees
On December 8, 2023 it was referred to the Health Subcommittee, and the congressional record shows no further action, no hearing, no markup, and no vote for the rest of the 118th Congress
The bill attracted 22 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, and none in the Senate
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill expired without coming up in either chamber

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The firearms industry and opponents of new gun regulation: no federal licensing system, no assault weapons or silencer ban, no excise tax increase, no repeal of industry legal protections, and no new dealer requirements took effect. Communities affected by gun violence remain without the prevention programs the bill would have funded.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The firearms industry and gun-rights groups

against.name: Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: His committee received the referral on December 5, 2023 and took no further action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — during the rest of the Congress

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Opposes federal gun licensing, universal background checks, and assault weapons bans and pressures lawmakers against such measures

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors plus the sponsor were Democrats, no Republican signed on, and the Republican-led committees never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would ban assault weapons and silencers, raise excise taxes on firearms, subject dealers to inspections, employee checks, and reporting rules, repeal an industry legal shield, and let gun trace data be used in civil lawsuits. Its interest in keeping those measures off the books runs against the bill's public-safety purpose.
The bill directs the Consumer Product Safety Commission to write mandatory standards for gun locks and safes and requires secure storage of firearms, creating demand for compliant locking devices.
The bill authorizes a dedicated community violence intervention grant program and funding for gun violence research, which these groups and researchers would administer and use.
